prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength concept to its realisation at 10^-18 fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B013 with Katori and Ye as a single-part prize. The chair's observation is correct that every camp has the same shape: the strongest science carries the weakest attribution, or the reverse. Applying that test to the shortlist, B013 is the only entry where the achievement, the maturity and the credit all hold at once. The achievement is one idea with one demonstration: Katori's magic wavelength removes the lattice light shift so that many atoms can be interrogated simultaneously, and Ye's group converted this into 10^-18 uncertainty by controlling blackbody, collisional and higher-order lattice shifts and by ultrastable lasers. The result is reproduced in several laboratories and species, clock-to-clock comparisons already test relativity at the centimetre-redshift level, and it is the instrument behind tests of fundamental constants. Two names are named identically by every proposal. I do not need to cut anyone: nobody has to choose between collaborations of thousands or between five credited names. On the chair's question about a ranking criterion, I would put clarity of attribution and maturity ahead of breadth of impact, because breadth is exactly what makes B001 and B020 hard to credit in three names, and I would not want the prize to rest on a cut that members cannot agree on among themselves.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that a lattice clock may be read as a precision-measurement advance rather than a discovery of a new phenomenon, and that it leans on the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-ion work. A reasonable committee could say that the redefinition of the second should come first, and other strontium, ytterbium and ion-clock groups remain outside the credited names. Against that, B001 has much broader opening support (seven top-three rankings) and is the mature field Mehlig and Johansson describe as arguably overdue; if the committee settles the Zoller-or-Esslinger question, B001 could be the better prize. I also have to concede that B013 has only two explicit first-round supporters, so I cannot claim a majority for it.

responses.point: Mehlig proposes an experiment-only B001 prize (Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger), calls the field mature and arguably overdue, and notes that analogue quantum simulation has so far reproduced known physics more than it has solved an open problem.
responses.response: I agree with the maturity point and with your own caveat about new physics, and I take B001 seriously. The experiment-only trio is the cleanest of the B001 options, because it avoids the overlap with B011. But it still asks the committee to rank Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger on first Mott and fermionic Hubbard results, which you admit are partly intertwined, and to leave out Zoller and Jaksch, whose proposal is the origin of the lattice as a simulator. That is a cut that members disagree about, and Johansson in fact proposes a different third name. For B013 no such cut is needed, so I keep it ahead of B001 while keeping B001 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Johansson now prefers a mixed B001 prize (Bloch, Greiner, Zoller) and says that quantum advantage has not been decisively shown and that the redefinition of the second could make recognition of B013 early.
responses.response: I accept that B001 and B011 should not reward Cirac and Zoller twice, and your move to B001 resolves that overlap more neatly than the theory-only B011. But the mixed trio and Mehlig's experimental trio are two different prizes with different citations, so the support for B001 is split in substance. On timing, I still disagree. A clock at 10^-18 is a measured fact in independent laboratories, and the redefinition of the second is a consequence of that maturity, not a precondition for it. By your own argument that quantum advantage is still prospective, B001 is also the one with the more prospective element.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that B020 is the clearest case of nature supplying the decisive clue, that the 2013 prize left the experimental discovery unrecognised, and that the difficulty is only one of attribution, to be handled by honouring conception and leadership of ATLAS and CMS.
responses.response: I accept the scientific weight and the distinction from 2013. My difficulty is that the attribution problem, which you describe as one of how to credit, is for a prize the entire question. Your trio (Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni) and the Chair's trio (Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee) differ in who is credited and in what for: leadership at the announcement versus construction. You yourself concede that this choice is partly arbitrary, and I do not think a citation for leadership roles meets the standard of a specific discovery with identifiable authors. For that reason I keep B020 only as an alternative, and I would support it if the committee found a rule that members actually share.

responses.point: Olsson separates a field that is still evolving from a discovery that is uncertain, and says that if the committee wants more time she could support B001 or B013 instead of B041.
responses.response: That is a fair distinction and I accept it: the existence of correlated states in magic-angle graphene is not in doubt, and I rank B041 low mainly because it is outside my field, so I weigh my own assessment lightly on the science. My concern is the one you raise yourself, that Cao and Dean fall outside the three names, so the citation would need to credit the discovery without implying that the group leader alone made it. I am glad that you list B013 as a name you could support, and it suggests that the committee may find more common ground there than the first-round counts suggest.

responses.point: Lindroth asked where the boundary lies in the solid-state memory work and held her first-round position for B013 with Katori and Ye, stressing the invention together with the control of systematic shifts.
responses.response: We agree on the citation, and I think the wording should keep both elements: the magic-wavelength concept alone would be a proposal, and the demonstration at 10^-18 alone would be a technique. On your credit-gap question, beyond Katori and Ye I see no gap that a two-name prize could close; the other strontium, ytterbium and ion-clock groups belong in the maturity argument. On your earlier question about B003, I would not want to build a prize from it, since the memory, cavity and network threads are not a single achievement.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads optical lattice clocks as a physics discovery or as a measurement advance, and whether it prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second.
Whether the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-ion prize make a clock prize look like a continuation, and whether other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups create a credit gap in a two-person prize.
Whether B001 can be given a stable three-name credit (Zoller or Esslinger as the third name), which would make it a stronger competitor than B013.
I assess B020 and B041 largely outside my expertise and rely on colleagues' attribution and maturity arguments.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. B003 (light-matter quantum interfaces and quantum memories) is close to my own work on optical quantum memories in rare-earth-ion-doped crystals, and I no longer put it among my alternatives; I would recuse myself from deciding it. For B013, my profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory and Lund colleagues and WACQT/European quantum-memory collaborations, but no documented personal or institutional connection to Katori or Ye; the Hall link is background lineage for the clock field and is flagged for transparency only. For B001, B011, B020 and B041 I know of no specific conflict from the provided profile.
